einzeiler: The Taiping advance captures prosperous Suzhou as the Qing dynasty crumbles from within.
kurzfassung: As Taiping forces advance through Jiangnan, imperial officials flee or deny entry to their own superiors while retreating government troops plunder cities. Suzhou falls to the rebels without bloodshed, surprisingly emerging as a functional administrative center under Li Xiucheng. Meanwhile, foreign missionaries travel to rebel territory, returning with sympathetic reports that challenge prevailing British hostility toward the movement.
stichpunkte: Imperial commander He Guiqing orders guards to fire on a desperate crowd begging for city defense before fleeing.
Jiangsu governor Xu Youren shuts Suzhou's gates against his superior officer and later reports him for mass murder.
Retreating imperial troops under Ma Dejiao sack Suzhou four days before the enemy arrives, destroying confidence in the dynasty.
Suzhou falls without a fight on June 2, and Li Xiucheng establishes surprisingly stable civilian administration rather than wholesale destruction.
Zeng Guofan receives supreme authority but bypasses the eastern crisis to focus on strategic containment around Anqing.
British and American missionaries travel upriver, meeting rebel leaders and returning with accounts praising Taiping pragmatism.
Missionary wife Jane Edkins writes a private letter confessing sympathy for the rebel cause as they approach Shanghai.

clips.hook: A provincial governor locks out his supreme commander
clips.text: A local official weighed the consequences of letting his panicked superior enter and decided that refusal caused less damage than admitting a fugitive.

clips.hook: An army plunders the very city it was sent to protect
clips.text: Imperial soldiers looted a major urban center just days before the enemy arrived, teaching residents the true worth of government protection.

clips.hook: The greatest victory in the history of the Taiping movement
clips.text: The rebellion successfully captured China's economic heartland with minimal cost, marking the high-water mark of their campaign.

clips.hook: A rebel leader wishes he was still a humble preacher
clips.text: The second-in-command of the rebellion confessed that his happiest days were spent assisting a missionary rather than ruling an empire.

clips.hook: Refugees crowd the waterways fleeing toward an uncertain sanctuary
clips.text: Entire households moved eastward by boat toward the one city controlled by neither the rebels nor the defending dynasty.

beschreibung:
For a thousand years, Suzhou and Hangzhou stood as synonyms for the next best thing to Heaven itself. Well... that was before 1860. As of now, Hangzhou is a fire-gutted ruin, and Suzhou is next on the target list.

But the army that does the most damage… is not the invader. The Taiping arrive to find the dirty work done ahead of them, by the very Qing forces assigned to defend the great southern city, and a vast number of the city having decided to "take matters into their own hands." As such, when a party of missionaries sails upriver from Shanghai to find out just what happened to Suzhou, they'll have to wade through a literal riverful of the dead.

Time Period Covered:
May-Aug. 1860 CE

Major Historical Figures:

The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom:
Hong Xiuquan, the Heavenly King [1814–1864]
Hong Rengan, the Shield King (Gan Wang), Prime Minister [1822–1864]
Li Xiucheng, the Loyal King (Zhong Wang) [1823–1864]

The Qing:
The Xianfeng Emperor [1831–1861]
He Guiqing, Governor-General of Liangjiang [1816–1862]
Xu Youren, Governor of Jiangsu [d. 1860]
Zeng Guofan, Governor-General of Liangjiang (from June 8, 1860); commander, Hunan Army [1811–1872]
Ma Dezhao, Qing commander

The Foreign Missionaries:
Joseph Edkins, London Missionary Society [1823–1905]
Jane Edkins, his wife [1841-1863]
Griffith John, Welsh Congregationalist missionary [1831–1912]
James Legge, London Missionary Society, Hong Kong [1815–1897]
